definition: The dog-days of summer; the period of sultry, oppressive heat traditionally associated with the heliacal rising of Sirius, the Dog Star, spanning roughly early July through mid-August in the Northern Hemisphere.
etymology: From Latin canicula, a diminutive of canis, dog — literally a little dog, the affectionate nickname Romans gave to Sirius. When that bright star rose with the sun in late summer, they reasoned it was adding its own heat to the day, and so the blistering season took the name of the small bright hound blazing overhead.
usage: We are standing now at the threshold of the canícula, those languid weeks when the air itself seems to lose the will to move.
